title: Sequencing by Expansion (SBX) – a novel, high-throughput single-molecule sequencing technology
one_line: A preprint from the Roche/Stratos team describing Sequencing by Expansion, in which a DNA template is copied into a much longer surrogate polymer (an 'Xpandomer') whose bulky reporters are then read electrically as they translocate a nanopore on a CMOS sensor array.
key_claims: Template DNA is enzymatically copied using X-NTP nucleotide analogues, then chemically expanded so that each original base is represented by a spatially separated reporter along a single surrogate molecule.
Expansion stretches the base-to-base spacing far beyond native DNA, which the authors argue removes the crowding that limits signal resolution when native DNA is passed through a nanopore.

Reading is done as a single-molecule electrical measurement of the Xpandomer through nanopores on a high-density CMOS sensor chip, giving a platform the authors position as massively parallel and high-throughput.
Because the sequencing step reads a synthetic polymer rather than the DNA itself, base-calling signal is decoupled from native DNA chemistry and modification state.
The authors present the method as a general platform intended for short- and long-read applications on the same chemistry.
limitations: As a preprint, the work had not been peer reviewed at the time of the episode.
Accuracy, throughput and cost figures come from the developers' own platform rather than independent benchmarking against established sequencers.
Performance on difficult contexts (homopolymers, repeats, modified bases, low-input or degraded samples) is not established by third parties.
The chemistry requires specialised X-NTP analogues and a proprietary sensor chip, so reproducibility outside the originating group is untested.
Real-world application data (clinical samples, whole-genome assemblies from external labs) were not available.
open_questions: Independent head-to-head benchmarking of raw read accuracy, read length distribution and error profile against Illumina, PacBio and ONT on the same reference samples.
Whether the expansion/copy step introduces sequence-dependent bias or dropout across GC-extreme and repetitive regions.
Whether epigenetic modifications can be detected, given that the Xpandomer is a synthetic surrogate rather than the native strand.
Whether the CMOS nanopore array's stated throughput holds at production scale and at what per-genome cost.
